newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani minister resumes Afghan peace shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani minister resumes Afghan peace shuttle.

text.p: Pakistan's Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar flew to the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Sunday in a new attempt to broker peace talks between warring Afghan factions, a government official said.

He said Babar would hold talks with powerful Uzbek militia leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, and later fly to the southern city of Kandahar, headquarters of Mullah Mohammad Omar, leader of the Islamic Taleban movement.
Pakistan has called for an immediate ceasefire and peace talks aimed at forming a broad-based Afghan government.

The official said the Taleban had expressed a new willingness to talk to ousted government military chief Ahmed Shah Masood, whose forces were closing in on Kabul on Sunday, just three weeks after the Taleban drove them from the capital.
There was no immediate confirmation from the Taleban that they were ready to talk peace with Masood.
The hardline Islamists have previously demanded that he "return all government property" -- a reference to Masood's military equipment -- before any talks can take place.

"It is a big achievement to get agreement of different factions to sit together and initiate a serious dialogue to bring peace and reconciliation which seemed impossible a few weeks ago," Babar told reporters on Saturday.
Despite the peace talks, Dostum's forces provided artillery support that helped Masood's fighters recapture the vital Bagram military airbase, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, on Friday.
The capture of Bagram was the first joint operation between Masood and Dostum. But the Uzbek commander did not commit his infantry, in an apparent sign he was keeping his options open.
Last week Dostum signed a defence pact with Masood and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili.
Babar, thought to have close links with the Taleban since their abrupt emergence two years ago, arranged the first public contact between Taleban leaders and Dostum on Wednesday.
Those talks in Mazar-i-Sharif were followed by a further round in Kandahar on Thursday.
The Taleban had previously shunned Dostum because of his service in the former communist government led by president Najibullah, killed by the Taleban after they took Kabul.
Babar said on Saturday that there were acute shortages of food, medicine and clothing in Kabul and other parts of Afghanistan facing the onset of winter.
"It would be criminal negligence on the part of the world community if they failed to come forward and help the Afghans," he said.
